network.overall_strategy: This is a complete candidate reaction graph from specified C1-C3 organic feedstocks, not a demonstrated prebiotic synthesis. The supplied literature does not establish even one complete prebiotic lysine synthesis; therefore the ten pathways below are explicitly hypothetical, nonidentical reaction sequences, not ten validated routes or independent lines of evidence. They share a proposed cyanoacetate/acrylonitrile precursor module. Starting with cyanoacetate avoids the previous requirement for selective hydrolysis of a trinitrile, but its environmental supply remains an unresolved feedstock assumption. The strongest branch converts the alpha functionality into a hydantoin before reducing the terminal nitrile, thereby avoiding selective hydrogenation of an aminodinitrile and suppressing alpha-amine-mediated cyclization. Other branches test different orders of hydration, protection, hydrogenation and deprotection. Every numerical operating window is a proposed screening range unless explicitly stated otherwise; none establishes substrate-specific yield or selectivity. The physical scenario is an anoxic geothermal field with surface pools and connected, H2-bearing subsurface fractures. Transport between these compartments is possible in principle, but concentration, cyanide/sulfide removal, catalyst survival and acid-base compartmentalization are unresolved requirements, not assumed separation operations. No O2, enzymes, biological protecting groups or industrial activated reductants are used. Neutral molecular formulas represent connectivity; actual protonation follows local pH. Stoichiometric coefficients are omitted as requested, but balancing species are included. Sulfur is represented by S8 as net redox bookkeeping, not a demonstrated exclusive photochemical product. All stereogenic products are unspecified stereoisomer mixtures; lysine is expected to be racemic. Terminal byproducts use the permitted intermediate role. Product claims would require quantified recovery, authentic lysine and pipecolate standards, and orthogonal structural confirmation. HCN-polymer hydrolysates are excluded because their unresolved molecular composition and contested lysine assignments cannot supply a defensible species-resolved pathway.

reactions.name: Candidate cyanoacetate Michael addition to acrylonitrile

conditions.catalyst: Hydroxide supplied by alkaline pool chemistry
conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 9.5-11; each organic substrate 1-30 mM; residence 1-30 days; anoxic, optically shielded porewater adjoining an evaporitic pool. Monitor acrylonitrile polymerization, cyanoacetate decarboxylation and nitrile hydrolysis.

reactions.mechanism: A small equilibrium population of the carbon-centered cyanoacetate nucleophile adds to the beta carbon of acrylonitrile; protonation produces NC-CH(COOH)-CH2-CH2-CN.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative: the supplied literature does not demonstrate this substrate pair under prebiotic conditions. An activated methylene donor is chemically preferable to assuming efficient acetaldehyde C-cyanoethylation. Starting with cyanoacetate also removes a required selective trinitrile-hydrolysis step. However, useful carbon deprotonation at geological alkalinity, productive addition and environmental cyanoacetate supply remain unverified. This is a changed bottleneck, not an established solution.

reactions.name: Decarboxylative formation of the C5 dinitrile skeleton

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 3-5; substrate 0.1-20 mM; residence 1 hour-7 days in a warm, acidic geothermal pool. Acidification must occur by mixing with a separate acidic fluid; it is not assumed to occur spontaneously in rxn_001.

reactions.mechanism: Loss of carbon dioxide from the alpha-cyano carboxylic acid gives a nitrile-stabilized carbon intermediate, followed by protonation to glutaronitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative for this substrate and operating window; no supporting experiment is supplied. Alpha-cyano-acid decarboxylation provides a recognizable mechanism and the correct carbon skeleton without selective cleavage of an unactivated C-C bond. Competing nitrile hydrolysis and the rate at the proposed temperatures require measurement.

reactions.name: Candidate photoredox monoreduction of glutaronitrile
agents: Dissolved Cu(I)-cyanide complexes as candidate photoredox catalysts

conditions.catalyst: Cu(I)-cyanide complexes; active speciation must be measured
conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 7.5-9; glutaronitrile 1-20 mM; total sulfide 0.1-5 mM; dissolved copper 1-100 micromolar; UV 240-280 nm, including a 254 nm laboratory comparison; residence 0.1-24 hours. Compare shallow, short-residence flow with batch irradiation. Copper-sulfide precipitation and second-end reduction must be quantified.

reactions.mechanism: Photochemical electron transfer partially reduces one nitrile to an imine, whose hydrolysis gives the aldehyde and ammonia. Sulfide supplies reducing equivalents; S8 represents an idealized net sulfur oxidation product.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative substrate extension. Patel et al. (2015) support related copper-mediated cyanosulfidic nitrile-to-carbonyl chemistry, not glutaronitrile monoreduction or lysine synthesis. Symmetry does not forbid a monoaldehyde, but neither useful mono-conversion nor suppression of rxn_024 is established. Short residence is a selectivity hypothesis, not a demonstrated separation. Ranjan et al. (2018) also identify episodic sulfur availability as a geochemical limitation.

reactions.name: Strecker capture of the nitrile-masked C5 aldehyde

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 8-9; aldehyde 0.1-10 mM; total ammonia 0.05-0.5 M; total cyanide 1-30 mM; residence 1-72 hours. Use shaded porewater receiving photochemical effluent. Such ammonia enrichment and retention of volatile HCN are required assumptions. Residual sulfide and competing aldehyde reactions must be measured.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia forms an imine with the aldehyde; cyanide addition establishes the alpha-aminonitrile while the future epsilon nitrogen remains nitrile-masked.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative on 4-cyanobutanal, but based on established Strecker reaction logic. Green et al. (2023) discuss relevant aminonitrile chemistry and its ammonia, pH and product-distribution limitations. The supplied report proposes this substrate but gives no synthesis data. Masking avoids starting from freely cyclizing 5-aminopentanal; it does not establish precursor availability or aminonitrile yield.

reactions.name: Carbon-dioxide capture and hydantoin formation from the aminodinitrile

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 8-9.5; aminodinitrile 0.1-10 mM; total dissolved inorganic carbon 20-200 mM; total ammonia 0.05-0.5 M; residence 1-14 days. CO2 denotes the equilibrating dissolved inorganic-carbon pool, predominantly bicarbonate at these pH values.

reactions.mechanism: Carbamate formation, intramolecular attack involving the alpha nitrile, and rearrangement produce a hydantoin. The net transformation adds CO2 without net water consumption.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative for this aminodinitrile. Pulletikurti et al. (2022) demonstrate related hydantoin-mediated amino-acid chemistry on different substrates, not this conversion. This branch deliberately differentiates the alpha functionality before hydrogenation and reduces alpha-nitrogen nucleophilicity. Hydantoin identity, distal-nitrile retention and the competing hydrolysis distribution need direct verification.

reactions.name: Protected terminal-nitrile hydrogenation at the hydantoin stage
agents: Awaruite, Ni3Fe, with exposed metallic Ni-rich surface sites; candidate catalyst

conditions.pressure: 50-150 bar total; H2 partial pressure 5-30 bar
conditions.catalyst: Awaruite Ni3Fe; activity and surface state unvalidated for this substrate
conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 8.5-10; substrate 0.1-5 mM; total ammonia 0.05-0.5 M; catalyst loading 1-20 g/L equivalent exposed mineral; residence 1-72 hours in an H2-bearing fracture. Measure dissolved H2, accessible Ni sites, adsorption and sulfur/cyanide inhibition. Transport from the surface module does not establish removal of catalyst poisons.

reactions.mechanism: Candidate metallic-Ni sites activate H2 and hydrogenate the terminal nitrile through imine intermediates to a primary amine while retaining both hydantoin carbonyls.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative and indispensable: no supplied study demonstrates this substrate on awaruite or another geologically supported catalyst. The mineral is selected as a natural Ni-bearing metallic phase, not because FeS-mediated keto-acid amination proves nitrile hydrogenation. Hydantoin protection is a genuine mechanistic improvement over an unprotected aminonitrile, but carbonyl reduction, secondary amination, adsorption and poisoning remain unresolved. Thoma and Powner (2023) explicitly leave lysine synthesis unsolved.

reactions.name: Ring opening of lysine hydantoin

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 10-11; substrate 0.1-5 mM; residence 1-14 days; high water activity. Transfer to a mineral-poor outlet zone is proposed, but desorption from the hydrogenation catalyst must be demonstrated.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolytic cleavage of the hydantoin acyl-nitrogen bond exposes the alpha carboxyl group while retaining the alpha-N-carbamoyl group.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative operating window for lysine hydantoin. Hydantoin opening is conventional chemistry and related hydantoin pathways appear in Pulletikurti et al. (2022), but neither useful conversion nor selectivity at geological alkalinity is established here. Product carbamoyl transfer, alternative ring cleavage and decomposition must be distinguished analytically.

reactions.name: Hydrolytic decarbamoylation to free lysine

conditions.catalyst: Hydronium in an acidic geothermal fluid
conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 1.5-3; substrate 0.1-5 mM; residence 1-30 days; water activity above 0.98. Requires a separate acidic fracture, not the alkaline hydrogenation fluid. Test rapid cooling of discharged products to 300-315 K. These conditions are not an established product-compatible window.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis removes the alpha-N-carbamoyl group, releasing ammonia and carbon dioxide and leaving lysine.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative and potentially rate-limiting. The supplied literature gives no nonenzymatic, substrate-specific demonstration of productive decarbamoylation to lysine under these conditions. High water activity and protonation may reduce cyclization relative to hot drying, but cannot guarantee survival. Re-formation of hydantoin and decomposition must be measured. The unresolved synthesis and competing lactam chemistry are emphasized by Thoma and Powner (2023).

reactions.name: Hydantoin opening before terminal-nitrile hydrogenation

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 10-11; substrate 0.1-10 mM; residence 1-30 days. Sample a time course for ring opening versus terminal-nitrile hydration and hydrolysis. No selective endpoint is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Hydantoin hydrolysis forms an N-carbamoyl alpha-amino acid while retaining the distal nitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative substrate-specific selectivity. Pulletikurti et al. (2022) support the broader hydantoin/amino-acid connection, not preferential ring opening with this terminal nitrile intact. This branch retains alpha-N protection during later hydrogenation but introduces an additional hydrolysis competition relative to P1.

reactions.name: Terminal-nitrile hydrogenation of the N-carbamoyl amino acid
agents: Awaruite, Ni3Fe, with exposed metallic Ni-rich surface sites; candidate catalyst

conditions.pressure: 50-150 bar total; H2 partial pressure 5-30 bar
conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 8.5-10; substrate 0.1-5 mM; total ammonia 0.05-0.5 M; mineral loading 1-20 g/L; residence 1-72 hours. Quantify carboxylate adsorption, catalyst inhibition and retention of the carbamoyl group.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrogenation converts the terminal nitrile to an aminomethyl group while the alpha nitrogen remains carbamoylated.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative: no supplied paper establishes this reduction on a natural metallic catalyst. Alpha-N protection should reduce intramolecular capture of partially reduced nitrile intermediates, but that advantage does not establish catalyst turnover or recovery of soluble product. This branch must be compared experimentally with hydantoin-stage reduction rather than assumed equivalent.

reactions.name: Candidate selective hydration of the alpha-aminonitrile

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 2-4; substrate 0.1-10 mM; residence 1 hour-14 days in shaded acidic porewater. Measure hydration of both nitriles, subsequent amide hydrolysis and acid-induced aminonitrile decomposition.

reactions.mechanism: Water addition to the alpha nitrile followed by proton transfers gives the alpha aminoamide.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative selectivity, not an established property of this dinitrile. Aminonitrile hydration is chemically credible, and Green et al. (2023) discuss related hydration/hydrolysis complexity. Electronic differentiation does not guarantee that the alpha nitrile hydrates usefully before the distal nitrile. This branch is retained as a testable alternative, not as an assumed selective preparation.

reactions.name: Thermal generation of the cyanate pool from urea

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 7.5-9; urea 0.05-0.5 M; residence 1-30 days in a concentrated, shaded pool. HNCO represents an equilibrating pool predominantly present as cyanate at this pH. Quantify steady-state cyanate rather than assuming complete urea conversion.

reactions.mechanism: Aqueous urea interconverts with ammonia and isocyanic acid/cyanate; subsequent trapping can draw on the minor reactive pool.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative as a productive geochemical supply module in this network; the supplied research provides no quantitative demonstration under these conditions. Urea/cyanate interconversion is ordinary chemistry, but cyanate hydrolysis, reverse urea formation and the required urea concentration may limit flux. This node supplies the carbon and nitrogen used in the separate carbamoylation reactions.

reactions.name: Cyanate carbamoylation of the nitrile-bearing aminoamide

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 7.5-8.5; aminoamide 0.1-10 mM; measured cyanate pool 0.1-20 mM; residence 1-72 hours. Use actual rxn_012 effluent rather than assuming purified cyanate. Competing ammonia capture must be quantified.

reactions.mechanism: The alpha amino group attacks the electrophilic carbon of the HNCO/cyanate pool, producing the explicit N-carbamoyl aminoamide intermediate.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative on this substrate and feed mixture; no supporting experiment appears in the supplied research. Carbamoylation is chemically plausible because only one free primary amine is present, but competition with ammonia and cyanate hydrolysis can dominate. The carbamoylated intermediate is represented explicitly rather than hiding protection and ring closure in one transformation.

reactions.name: Cyclization of the N-carbamoyl aminoamide to the masked hydantoin

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 3-5; substrate 0.1-10 mM; residence 1-14 days. Requires acidification after carbamoylation. Monitor competing hydrolysis to the N-carbamoyl acid and distal-nitrile loss.

reactions.mechanism: Intramolecular attack by the carbamoyl nitrogen on the alpha amide carbonyl closes the five-membered hydantoin ring with ammonia elimination.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative under the stated aqueous conditions. Five-membered-ring formation supplies a recognizable mechanism, but ammonia elimination from an amide may be too slow at these temperatures. Pulletikurti et al. (2022) provide related hydantoin precedent, not evidence for this particular cyclization. Separating this step from rxn_013 exposes its independent kinetic requirement.

reactions.name: Alpha-amide hydrolysis with attempted distal-nitrile retention

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 1.5-3; substrate 0.1-10 mM; residence 1-30 days. The same acidity can attack the distal nitrile; evaluate full product distributions rather than a single endpoint.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis replaces the alpha amide nitrogen with hydroxyl, releasing ammonia and producing the nitrile-bearing amino acid.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative selective conversion; the elementary amide hydrolysis is conventional, but no supplied study establishes distal-nitrile survival on this substrate. The proposed conditions may give little conversion or substantial aminoadipate instead. This requirement makes P5, P6 and P8 less secure than hydrogenation of a preformed hydantoin.

reactions.name: Late alpha-N carbamoylation of the nitrile-bearing amino acid

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 7.5-8.5; amino acid 0.1-10 mM; measured cyanate pool 0.1-20 mM; residence 1-72 hours. Requires neutralization of rxn_015 effluent by a distinct alkaline fluid; dilution and salt effects must be measured.

reactions.mechanism: The alpha amine captures the cyanate-derived carbamoyl group, restoring reduced alpha-nitrogen nucleophilicity before hydrogenation.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative substrate-specific application of ordinary cyanate carbamoylation; no direct supporting study is supplied. This creates a chemically meaningful protection alternative rather than requiring selective reduction of two nitriles. Its feasibility still depends on selective production of mol_022 and sustained cyanate availability.

reactions.name: Cyclodehydration of the N-carbamoyl nitrile-bearing amino acid
agents: Brønsted acidity retained in the concentrating film

conditions.catalyst: Brønsted acid sites or dissolved acid concentrated during drying; no specific mineral assumed
conditions.other: Proposed screen: begin with pH 2-4 solution, then lower water activity to 0.1-0.3; residence 1-48 hours per drying cycle. Bulk pH is not defined in the dry film. Rehydrate and measure hydantoin recovery and nitrile integrity.

reactions.mechanism: Intramolecular condensation of the carbamoyl nitrogen with the alpha carboxyl group forms the five-membered hydantoin and eliminates water.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative operating window. This is the dehydrative reverse of hydantoin opening, with reduced water activity providing a chemical driving factor. Drying alone does not establish useful conversion; competing decomposition and incomplete ring closure remain possible. No substrate-specific experiment is supplied.

reactions.name: Early decarbamoylation with attempted terminal-nitrile retention

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 1.5-3; substrate 0.1-5 mM; residence 1-30 days; high water activity. Quantify distal-nitrile hydrolysis concurrently. No selective deprotection window is known.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolytic removal of the carbamoyl group releases ammonia and carbon dioxide, leaving an unprotected alpha amine and a terminal nitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative and particularly low confidence. No supplied paper establishes carbamoyl removal while retaining this nitrile. Conditions adequate for deprotection may also destroy the intended reducible group, and early deprotection restores the risk of reductive cyclization during rxn_021. P9 and P10 are explicit adverse-selectivity tests, not equivalent alternatives to P1.

reactions.name: Unprotected terminal-nitrile hydrogenation at the aminoamide stage
agents: Awaruite, Ni3Fe, with exposed metallic Ni-rich surface sites; candidate catalyst

conditions.pressure: 50-150 bar total; H2 partial pressure 5-30 bar
conditions.catalyst: Awaruite Ni3Fe; activity and selectivity unvalidated
conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 8.5-10; substrate 0.1-5 mM; total ammonia 0.05-0.5 M; mineral loading 1-20 g/L; residence 1-72 hours. Monitor cyclic products, secondary amines and reduction of the alpha amide.

reactions.mechanism: Candidate metal-catalyzed hydrogenation converts the remaining nitrile to a primary amine without reducing the alpha amide.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative: no supplied work validates this substrate-catalyst combination. Converting the alpha nitrile to an amide removes dinitrile hydrogenation selectivity, but the free alpha amine can capture a partially reduced distal nitrile and cause cyclization. Amide retention and primary-amine selectivity must be demonstrated separately.

reactions.name: Lysinamide hydrolysis to lysine

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 1.5-3; substrate 0.1-5 mM; residence 1-14 days; high water activity followed by cooling to 300-315 K. Acidic fluid must be physically separated from the metallic hydrogenation zone.

reactions.mechanism: Acid-catalyzed hydrolysis of the carboxamide gives lysine and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative prebiotic operating window, although the amide-to-acid transformation is conventional. This step is meaningful only if authentic lysinamide is first demonstrated in rxn_019. No supplied study reports lysine recovery from this sequence, and protonation does not eliminate thermal degradation. Thoma and Powner (2023) emphasize that downstream lysine chemistry is not evidence of lysine synthesis.

reactions.name: Unprotected terminal-nitrile hydrogenation to lysine
agents: Awaruite, Ni3Fe, with exposed metallic Ni-rich surface sites; candidate catalyst

conditions.pressure: 50-150 bar total; H2 partial pressure 5-30 bar
conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 8.5-10; substrate 0.1-5 mM; total ammonia 0.05-0.5 M; mineral loading 1-20 g/L; residence 1-72 hours. Determine lysine/pipecolate branching, dissolved-product recovery and inhibition by carried-over cyanide or sulfide.

reactions.mechanism: Complete hydrogenation of the distal nitrile gives the epsilon primary amine if intermolecular hydrogen delivery outcompetes intramolecular alpha-amine capture.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative and lower confidence than protected hydrogenation. Neither catalyst activity nor productive branching is established in the supplied research. The atom-balanced lysine endpoint does not show that it predominates over rxn_025. The report's cyclization critique is therefore treated as an explicit competing pathway rather than assumed away.

reactions.name: Competing terminal-nitrile hydrolysis to alpha-aminoadipic acid

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 1.5-3; substrate 0.1-5 mM; residence 1-30 days. This is a loss-channel screen under conditions overlapping acidic hydrolysis and deprotection.

reactions.mechanism: Sequential nitrile hydration and amide hydrolysis replace the terminal nitrile with a carboxyl group and release ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative rate and branching under these conditions, but a chemically conventional competitor. Alpha-aminoadipate is not declared an irreversible chemical dead end; it is a sink relative to this target-producing graph because reducing its unactivated terminal carboxyl group would require another unsupported module. The supplied report specifically identifies that carboxyl-reduction gap.

reactions.name: Potential lysine loss by lactamization during drying

conditions.other: Proposed loss screen: solution initially pH 7-9, followed by water activity below 0.1; residence 1-30 days over repeated drying cycles. Bulk pH is undefined after drying. This is not a measured rate window for free lysine.

reactions.mechanism: Intramolecular epsilon-amine attack on the carboxyl group, followed by dehydration, can form a seven-membered amino lactam.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative significance at the stated surface temperatures. Thoma and Powner (2023) demonstrate important lactam competition for activated lysine derivatives, not a free-lysine loss rate in this film. The supplied industrial evidence concerns hotter, nonaqueous conditions and cannot establish substantial loss here. This reaction is included to test preservation, not to assert that lactamization necessarily dominates.

reactions.name: Competing second-end photoreduction to glutaraldehyde
agents: Dissolved Cu(I)-cyanide complexes as candidate photoredox catalysts

conditions.other: Proposed screen matching rxn_003: pH 7.5-9; total sulfide 0.1-5 mM; copper 1-100 micromolar; UV 240-280 nm; residence 0.1-24 hours. Measure aldehyde photochemistry and secondary condensation as additional unenumerated losses.

reactions.mechanism: Photoreduction and hydrolysis of the remaining nitrile produce a second aldehyde, eliminating the nitrogen mask needed by the proposed target sequence.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative substrate extension of the reaction family in Patel et al. (2015). If rxn_003 is possible, continued conversion of its monoaldehyde product is an obvious competing possibility, but its rate cannot be inferred from symmetry alone. Including this sink prevents short-residence operation from being mistaken for established monoselectivity.

reactions.name: Competing reductive cyclization to pipecolic acid
agents: Awaruite, Ni3Fe, with exposed metallic Ni-rich surface sites; candidate catalyst

conditions.pressure: 50-150 bar total; H2 partial pressure 5-30 bar
conditions.other: Proposed screen matching rxn_021: pH 8.5-10; substrate 0.1-5 mM; total ammonia 0.05-0.5 M; mineral loading 1-20 g/L; residence 1-72 hours. Quantify pipecolic acid with an authentic standard alongside lysine.

reactions.mechanism: Partial terminal-nitrile reduction generates an imine susceptible to intramolecular alpha-amine capture. Ammonia elimination and further hydrogenation yield the six-membered cyclic amino acid.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative substrate-catalyst realization, but chemically motivated by the supplied report's amino-carbonyl cyclization problem. This explicit competitor explains why unprotected nitrile hydrogenation is not assumed to furnish lysine selectively. Neither Huber and Wächtershäuser (2003) nor Muchowska et al. (2019), which concern different amination chemistry, establishes the lysine/pipecolate branching ratio.

pathways.name: Hydantoin-first protection and hydrogenation
pathways.description: Highest-priority hypothesis: construct the masked aldehyde, perform Strecker capture, form a CO2-derived hydantoin, reduce the only remaining nitrile, then open and deprotect. Avoids both dinitrile hydrogenation selectivity and free-alpha-amine hydrogenation. Precursor production, mineral catalysis and product-compatible deprotection remain unvalidated.

pathways.name: Hydantoin entry followed by protected open-chain hydrogenation
pathways.description: Open the CO2-derived hydantoin before reducing the distal nitrile, retaining alpha-N carbamoylation. Compared with P1, this additionally requires hydantoin opening without significant nitrile hydrolysis and productive hydrogenation of an adsorbing carboxylate substrate.

pathways.name: Aminoamide and cyanate entry into hydantoin-first hydrogenation
pathways.description: Hydrate the alpha nitrile, generate cyanate from urea, carbamoylate the aminoamide, and separately cyclize it to the protected hydantoin before hydrogenation. Explicitly tests hydration selectivity, cyanate supply and ammonia-eliminating ring closure.

pathways.name: Cyanate-derived hydantoin followed by protected open-chain hydrogenation
pathways.description: Use the explicit aminoamide-carbamoylation/cyclization entry, then open the hydantoin before reduction. Retains alpha-N protection but combines the cyanate-entry uncertainties with selective hydantoin opening.

pathways.name: Amino-acid-first formation with late carbamoyl protection
pathways.description: Hydrolyze the alpha functionality to the amino acid, then carbamoylate its alpha nitrogen before nitrile reduction. Avoids obligatory hydantoin formation but requires preserving the distal nitrile through two hydrolytic operations.

pathways.name: Late carbamoylation and dehydrative hydantoin formation
pathways.description: Produce the nitrile-bearing amino acid, carbamoylate it, and use cyclodehydration to enter the hydantoin-protected hydrogenation branch. This tests a chemically distinct ring-forming entry, not an assumed benefit of arbitrary environmental cycling.

pathways.name: Aminoamide-stage unprotected hydrogenation
pathways.description: Hydrate the alpha nitrile, reduce the remaining nitrile without alpha-N protection, then hydrolyze lysinamide. This shorter sequence avoids dinitrile hydrogenation but leaves a substantial reductive-cyclization risk.

pathways.name: Amino-acid-stage unprotected hydrogenation
pathways.description: Complete alpha-nitrile hydrolysis before reducing the distal nitrile directly to lysine. Explicitly competes with terminal-nitrile hydrolysis to aminoadipate and reductive cyclization to pipecolate; productive branching is unknown.

pathways.name: CO2-derived hydantoin with complete deprotection before reduction
pathways.description: Use hydantoin chemistry to establish the alpha carboxyl group, remove protection while retaining the distal nitrile, and then hydrogenate. Particularly low confidence because early decarbamoylation must spare the nitrile and forfeits protection against reductive cyclization.

pathways.name: Cyanate-derived hydantoin with complete deprotection before reduction
pathways.description: Enter through selective aminoamide formation and explicit cyanate carbamoylation/cyclization, then fully deprotect before final hydrogenation. This is a distinct but low-confidence sequence combining cyanate-entry bottlenecks with nitrile-preserving deprotection and unprotected reduction.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The strongest proposed route on mechanistic grounds. Hydantoin formation consumes the alpha-nitrile and decreases alpha-nitrogen nucleophilicity before terminal-nitrile reduction, addressing two genuine selectivity problems. However, rxn_003 has no demonstrated useful accumulation or trapping of the monoaldehyde, and rxn_006 lacks an identified, environmentally supported hydrogenation catalyst. The final hydrolyses are chemically reasonable, but conditions establishing lysine recovery rather than competing degradation are absent.
suggestions: Measure the glutaronitrile photoreduction product distribution and determine whether in-situ Strecker trapping can capture sufficient mol_012 before further reduction or other aldehyde reactions.

Demonstrate rxn_005 through rxn_008 sequentially with an identified H2-activating catalyst, realistic carry-over conditions, and quantified lysine recovery. Explicitly test cyanide and sulfide effects on catalyst activity.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The route is structurally coherent and retains alpha-N protection during hydrogenation. Nevertheless, surface hydantoin opening in rxn_009 requires an unspecified hydrolytic window that preserves the distal nitrile. Hydrogenation of the resulting N-carbamoyl amino acid is plausible in principle, but catalyst compatibility, protection-group survival and competing hydrolysis have not been established. A hydrothermal label alone does not establish these requirements.
suggestions: Establish the temperature, pH and residence-time window for rxn_009 while measuring both hydantoin opening and distal-nitrile hydrolysis.
Test mol_019 hydrogenation in the actual ring-opening matrix, monitoring carbamoyl retention, catalyst activity and subsequent lysine recovery.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Cyanate carbamoylation provides a chemically credible alternative entry to the protected intermediate. The unresolved requirements are selective alpha-aminonitrile hydration in rxn_011, sufficient cyanate activity from rxn_012, and cyclization of the primary carboxamide with ammonia loss in rxn_014. Once mol_015 forms, the route inherits P1's unresolved hydrogenation and lysine-recovery requirements. Urea availability alone does not establish an effective cyanate supply.
suggestions: Measure positional hydration selectivity for mol_014, including terminal-nitrile hydration and further hydrolysis products.

Quantify the HNCO/OCN- pool generated from urea under stated surface conditions and demonstrate mol_028-to-mol_015 conversion despite competing cyanate hydrolysis, ammonia capture and condensation chemistry.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The cyanate-derived hydantoin and subsequent N-carbamoyl amino acid are correctly connected. Cyclization followed by ring opening is not intrinsically invalid, but the submission does not specify conditions that make rxn_014 and rxn_009 productive at their respective stages while retaining the distal nitrile. The selective hydration and cyanate-supply uncertainties remain, followed by unsupported substrate-specific hydrogenation in rxn_010.
suggestions: Determine the kinetic and equilibrium windows for hydantoin formation and opening, including nitrile retention throughout both operations.
Demonstrate the cyanate-to-hydrogenation sequence with realistic carry-over or physically justified transfers rather than assuming purified mol_019 reaches the subsurface catalyst.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Late carbamoylation is a plausible way to suppress alpha-amine participation during the subsequent reduction. Its usefulness depends on first obtaining mol_022 through rxn_011 and rxn_015 while retaining the terminal nitrile. No relative hydrolysis rates establish that window; amide hydrolysis cannot simply be assumed to spare the nitrile. Carbamoylation also does not protect intermediates during the preceding unprotected stages.
suggestions: Measure alpha-nitrile hydration, alpha-amide hydrolysis and distal-nitrile hydrolysis under the same proposed conditions, tracking all identifiable products.
Demonstrate productive carbamoylation of mol_022 in the hydrolysis mixture, followed by protected hydrogenation and deprotection with measured material recovery.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This route reaches the same protected hydrogenation substrate as P1 and therefore has a sound protection rationale. Its additional uncertainty comes from specific chemical requirements, not its step count: two selective hydrolytic transformations must precede carbamoylation, and rxn_017 requires a demonstrated cyclization window with suitable acidity and water activity. Formation of the hydantoin does not resolve the missing hydrogenation catalyst or final product-survival evidence.
suggestions: Demonstrate distal-nitrile retention through hydration, amide hydrolysis, carbamoylation and cyclization, rather than validating those transformations only on separate purified substrates.

Specify how the proposed surface setting supplies the conditions for rxn_017 and transfers the resulting material to an active hydrogenation environment without unaccounted concentration or purification.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Lysinamide hydrolysis is a credible final transformation if mol_023 can be obtained. The principal difficulty is rxn_019: partial terminal-nitrile hydrogenation creates imine chemistry accessible to the unprotected alpha-amine, providing a favorable six-membered-ring pathway toward pipecolamide rather than lysinamide. Protonation or reaction-medium effects might alter this competition, but neither an effective catalyst nor a demonstrated selectivity window is supplied.
suggestions: Test mol_020 hydrogenation with authentic lysinamide and pipecolamide standards, including the cyclic-amide branch in product accounting.
Determine whether environmentally justified pH, ammonia activity and catalyst conditions permit sufficient lysinamide recovery for rxn_020.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The formal carbon skeleton and final product assignment are correct, but the route combines unverified differential hydrolysis with unprotected terminal-nitrile hydrogenation. In rxn_021, the alpha-amine can intercept partially reduced nitrile intermediates, enabling the explicitly included pipecolate branch rxn_025. Terminal-nitrile hydrolysis through rxn_022 also competes. No conditions establish useful lysine recovery among these outcomes.
suggestions: Measure rxn_021, rxn_022 and rxn_025 under identical catalyst, H2, pH and temperature conditions using authentic lysine, pipecolate and alpha-aminoadipate standards.
Establish sufficient mol_022 formation and distal-nitrile retention across rxn_011 and rxn_015 before evaluating the final hydrogenation as a complete route.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Hydantoin entry is chemically plausible, but complete deprotection before hydrogenation removes the protection exactly when intramolecular imine capture becomes important. Additionally, rxn_018 assumes carbamoyl hydrolysis while retaining the terminal nitrile, without a demonstrated kinetic window. The graph reaches lysine formally, but this branch does not retain P1's mechanistic advantage during the decisive reduction.
suggestions: Measure decarbamoylation relative to terminal-nitrile hydrolysis under the proposed hydrothermal conditions.
Demonstrate lysine recovery from unprotected mol_022 against pipecolate formation; if this competition cannot be controlled, retain alpha-N protection during hydrogenation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The intermediates form a valid formal route, but cyanate-derived hydantoin formation is followed by removal of protection before the problematic reduction. Selective hydration, cyanate availability, aminoamide cyclization and nitrile-preserving decarbamoylation are all unvalidated for this sequence. The final step therefore retains the same lysine-versus-pipecolate uncertainty as P8 and P9; successful hydantoin formation would not establish successful lysine synthesis.
suggestions: Confirm mol_015, mol_019 and mol_022 from the sequential cyanate route with structural measurements that establish retention of the distal nitrile.
Evaluate the final unprotected hydrogenation independently and then in the upstream reaction matrix, quantifying lysine, pipecolate, hydrolysis products and unrecovered material.

evaluation.network_feedback:
Not approved at the required network confidence threshold of 0.90. Structural validity is excellent: the 28 molecule nodes and 25 reaction nodes form a connected network, all listed species are reachable from the declared inputs, molecule IDs are consistent, and the formal routes produce the correctly identified lysine skeleton. The supplied deterministic check is accepted as ground truth: all 25 reactions conserve atoms and charge with the permitted coefficients. No reaction is designated problematic for a conservation violation. The coefficients of eight in rxn_003 and rxn_024 arise from S8 bookkeeping and are not intrinsically implausible; they do not establish the actual sulfur-product distribution. Racemic lysine satisfies the stated target.

The principal limitations are chemical selectivity and environmental implementation, not graph size, pathway count, shared intermediates or environment order. The cyanoacetate Michael addition and decarboxylation are reasonable reaction classes, although rxn_001 needs conditions supporting productive C-addition without excessive multiple addition or competing feedstock reactions. The essential common bottleneck is rxn_003: no substrate-specific evidence establishes sufficient 4-cyanobutanal formation and capture. A second essential requirement is terminal-nitrile hydrogenation. H2 availability alone does not establish a useful reaction rate or selectivity; rxn_006 and rxn_010 require an identified active catalyst, while rxn_019 and rxn_021 additionally expose the substrate to intramolecular reductive cyclization. Hydantoin-first protection addresses real mechanistic risks but does not demonstrate that these requirements have been met.

Environmental consistency remains underdetermined. Reaction entries provide Surface or Hydrothermal labels but no numerical temperature, pH, pressure, residence time, concentration, catalyst-phase or irradiation specifications. Connected pools and fractures make transport physically conceivable, but do not establish solute retention, concentration, acid-base transitions or catalyst compatibility with cyanide and sulfide carry-over. Declared starting materials are accepted as graph boundary conditions; their use is not itself penalized. Their activities and persistence in the proposed environments nevertheless require justification.

The competing edges are chemically relevant and should not be counted as successful target production. Indicative feasibility scores are rxn_022: 0.78, rxn_023: 0.78, rxn_024: 0.40 and rxn_025: 0.60. Nitrile hydrolysis and drying-induced lactamization are credible sinks, although their rates require measurement under the actual conditions. Second-end photoreduction remains an unvalidated extension of rxn_003, and reductive cyclization requires an active reduction system. Their inclusion improves the accounting of possible outcomes but does not establish a favorable lysine material balance.

Literature alignment is moderate: the proposal accurately acknowledges the lack of a validated complete route and incorporates important cyclization and stability concerns. Patel et al. (2015) and Pulletikurti et al. (2022) provide relevant reaction-class analogies, not experimental validation of these particular substrates and sequences. The reaction entries themselves lack citations connecting individual transformations to substrate-specific conditions or results. Absence of a prior lysine synthesis is not a mechanistic disproof; the low confidence follows the unresolved essential reactions and their integration. A modest-yield mixture could still establish success, but it requires quantified lysine recovery with authentic standards and orthogonal structural confirmation. Overall confidence reflects those essential requirements rather than averaging ancillary reactions or treating the ten pathways as independent evidence.
